hints.quote: Do not look at your periodontal chart and see where you have [4s and 5s] and assign the stage based on your probing depth, because that could be incorrect. You may over-diagnose a case that does not even have periodontitis, just because a patient has a bunch of 4s and 5s.
hints.take: Never assign a stage from probing depth alone — confirm attachment loss and bone loss first. This was repeated twice in lecture, which is normally a signal of exam importance.

hints.quote: And never forget this, is caries control is part of Phase I.
hints.take: Caries control is bundled into Phase I therapy, not deferred until after SRP or surgery.

hints.quote: These are must-pass to pass the course, irrespective of what your grade is... you may have a 95 on the final grade, but you still have to pass these three things.
hints.take: The three PCD competencies — charting/probing, identifying and selecting instruments, and scaling/root planing — must each be passed on their own, separate from your overall course grade.

hints.quote: It's fair to come back and ask you [about session 1–4 material on the final]. These are things you're going to be doing on your patients day in and day out, here and later.
hints.take: The comprehensive final can re-test material already covered on the midterm — do not treat midterm topics as "done" once the midterm has passed.

hints.quote: The evidence is overwhelming for the efficacy of periodontal maintenance.
hints.take: Be ready to cite the Becker et al. tooth-loss-per-year figures (untreated vs. treated-without-maintenance vs. treated-with-maintenance) as the evidence base for this claim.

hints.quote: Nothing really in the minutiae of things such as percentages and all that. You may have one or two on those, but that's not really the gist of it.
hints.take: Exam questions lean case-based and conceptual rather than testing exact epidemiological percentages — know the concepts (e.g., "42% of US adults have some form of periodontitis") without over-memorizing statistics.

hints.quote: Third molars aren't always kind of taking an account in the essence of the case because they're not always present for most patients... we typically don't necessarily take them heavily into account.
hints.take: When staging a case, third-molar findings (like isolated mobility) usually will not drive the overall stage the way the same finding on another tooth would.

hints.quote: There's a lot of incisions that we have, but I will focus on only two: vertical and crestal incisions... We have different kinds of incisions, but we're not going to go deep into those kind of incisions.
hints.take: Study intrasulcular/crestal and vertical incisions in depth — other incision families were named only in passing and aren't where this lecture's testing weight sits.

hints.quote: This topic is very controversial... it's really a topic that can be based on the clinician preference. Like, if you ask the same question or the same case for two different surgeons, they might have a different opinion on what's the best material of suture material we're going to use, what is the best incision or flap design we're going to be doing in this case.
hints.take: Expect case-based reasoning rather than a single memorized "correct" answer for incision/flap/suture choice — be ready to justify a defensible option, the same case-based exam style as Session 1.

hints.quote: One of the things that Dr. Ramsey asked me to talk about is basically a sub-marginal incision.
hints.take: Sub-marginal incision was added to the in-class follow-up at another instructor's explicit request — treat it as testable even though the original recording only promised depth on intrasulcular/crestal and vertical incisions.

hints.quote: What was question number one in your quiz? Where do you place your vertical incision? ...At the line [angle]... Why I cannot place it in the middle? ...It would lead to recession... If I place it in the middle of the papilla, what's going to happen? I might kill the papilla and you end up with a black triangle.
hints.take: Confirmed as a literal quiz question: vertical incisions go at the line angle, never through the papilla — placing one mid-papilla risks a black triangle, placing one off the line angle risks recession.

hints.quote: When we say trapezoidal flap that was another question exam or quiz... most of the time when you are doing your vertical incisions... the base always has to be wider than the upper part... so that the flap can survive.
hints.take: Confirmed as a literal quiz question: a flap's base must be wider than its coronal edge, or the flap starves the tissue it's still attached to of blood supply.

hints.quote: If I were a betting woman, but I'm not, but if I were a betting woman, I might think about these questions and our discussion about them and how that might inform the midterm.
hints.take: The in-class poll questions (McGuire & Nunn's driving factor, its accuracy, category order, diagnostic vs. therapeutic) are signaled as midterm material.

hints.quote: Those two questions that we just did on the slide now, and then the next thing that I'm going to mention are high likelihood questions for a midterm. What's the order of these prognostication categories? Good, fair, poor, questionable, hopeless.
hints.take: Know that McGuire & Nunn sorts by maintainability, its ~80% / ~50% accuracy figures, and the exact category order.

hints.quote: The mistake everybody makes is they want to flip-flop poor and questionable, right? Because it feels like poor is worse.
hints.take: In McGuire & Nunn, questionable comes after poor. A questionable tooth either gets worse (hopeless) or improves (poor).

hints.quote: Instead of memorizing the order, which we will then lay down on our pillow the night after the midterm and it will all flow out of our ear... let's think about what those two systems are based on.
hints.take: McGuire & Nunn is about tooth retention (diagnostic or therapeutic). Kwok & Caton is about periodontal stability (therapeutic only), which is why questionable sits in its middle.

hints.quote: Which of these can be used as a diagnostic prognostication system? Everybody in here should have the answer to that, right?
hints.take: Only McGuire & Nunn works as a diagnostic prognosis. Any of the three can be used therapeutically.

hints.quote: Don't Forget!!! 1. Modified Pen Grasp Technique 2. Finger Rest
hints.take: The one slide in the deck set in all-caps emphasis. Know the four finger rests (conventional, cross-arch, opposite-arch, finger-on-finger). From the slide deck. In class she deferred grasp and finger rests to the PCD sessions, so expect them there and on the practical.

hints.quote: Number of questions: around 40. Type of questions: A few Patient Box (case-based) scenarios with majority multiple choice questions, a few multiple answers (with partial credit) and matching questions. No essays.
hints.take: Dr. Abou-Arraj's midterm email (Oct 1, 10:00 am, sessions 1-4). Exam-day update: 46 questions in 80 minutes, no matching, and one ordering question (pick the right order of categories). Practice the format: the Mock Exam's midterm-format option mixes Patient Box cases, multiple-answer items with partial credit, one ordering question and MCQs. On multiple-answer items, pick only what you're sure of, since wrong picks can cost credit.

hints.quote: For the midterm exam, you will not be tested on instruments/ultrasonics/polishing. For exam preparation, focus on the discussion and slides up to failure of therapy in the given pdf.
hints.take: From Dr. Kaur's email the day after class. Everything in the deck after failure of therapy (instruments, ultrasonics, technique, polishing) is off the midterm. Those questions are tagged 'Not on midterm' and left out of the midterm mock exam. The email says nothing about the final, so don't drop them for good.

hints.quote: How many times you have seen this before? Has anybody been counting? That's going to be on the quiz.
hints.take: Said of the host-bacteria pathogenesis diagram (health → gingivitis → periodontitis). Know it cold: plaque bacteria initiate, the host response drives progression, and SRP targets the bacteria.

hints.quote: Bacteria is only responsible for 25% of the damage that happens in periodontitis. 75% of the damage that happens in periodontitis is because of those inflammatory markers and cells of bone destruction, osteoclasts, that are released by the host.
hints.take: The 25/75 split. Bacteria bring endotoxin (LPS), not osteoclasts. Removing them calms the host, and host modulation (Dr. Litz) calms it directly.

hints.quote: In health, pocket depth is not equal to clinical attachment level.
hints.take: The margin sits coronal to the CEJ, so recession is negative. CAL = PD + GR with its sign: PD 5, GR −3 → CAL 2.

hints.quote: Not putting anything for gingival recession will make you over-diagnose disease. Just putting zeros without calculating if there is a positive or negative gingival recession will also give you inaccurate diagnosis.
hints.take: In Salud a blank or a reflexive 0 sets CAL = PD. Skipped negative recession turns a CAL-2 site into CAL 5 and a false Stage 3/4.

hints.quote: Debridement is not a therapeutic procedure... debridement should never be combined with scaling and root planing.
hints.take: The only indication is calculus hiding the gingival margin so no numbers can be captured. Full-mouth code only; insurance won't pay for it plus an exam the same day (return in about 2 weeks).

hints.quote: Class 2 furcation is the one which is most amenable for regeneration... Class three is through and through. It's the most difficult one to treat.
hints.take: Glickman, not millimeters: I catch, II cul-de-sac (containable), III through-and-through, IV visible. Root caries in a Class IV furcation means a hopeless tooth.

hints.quote: Fremitus is palpated, not seen.
hints.take: Fremitus is mobility in function, felt with a finger on the root; it can be vertical and/or horizontal. Static mobility uses two blunt instruments, and a depressible tooth is ready for extraction.

hints.quote: We cannot assume by treating a 5 millimeter pocket on that site, we are going to resolve grade 2 mobility on that tooth, unless we address the underlying occlusal deformity.
hints.take: Occlusal trauma on a reduced periodontium (lack of posterior support, parafunction, overjet/overbite). Record occlusal findings in the notes section, since the chart has no field for them.

hints.quote: Sometimes the immediate response is to get rid of the pocket. That is not the rationale for doing scaling and root planing.
hints.take: The goals are less inflammation, a gram-negative → gram-positive shift and arrested progression. SRP does not reverse bone or attachment loss, even though PD drops.

hints.quote: Research has shown if we wait longer, we are not going to get any additional reduction in that pocket.
hints.take: Why re-evaluation is at 4-6 weeks: JE reattaches in 7-10 days, connective tissue in 4-6 weeks (collagen matures over 3-6 months).

hints.quote: If you have taken care of all the calculus and bacteria at the time of scaling and root planing, multiple sessions of scaling and root planing is not going to do anything. But what is going to work here is improvement in patient's oral hygiene.
hints.take: At re-eval, residual calculus → remove it and re-evaluate in 2 weeks. Otherwise the fix is home care, not more SRP.

hints.quote: If someone asks you, is scaling only for supra-G or sub-G? It's for both.
hints.take: Scaling is supra- and subgingival. Root planing is subgingival, on root surfaces only. Clinically they're done together.

hints.quote: Sometimes we end up using these terms interchangeably, they are completely different.
hints.take: Prophylaxis is preventive, for patients who never had periodontitis. Maintenance is supportive therapy after treated periodontitis, and localized SRP on residual pockets falls under it. D4346 sits between prophy and SRP.

hints.quote: The only thing the ultrasonic instruments cannot accomplish is root planing.
hints.take: Piezoelectric units work subgingivally too. Her sequence: ultrasonic for gross deposits → hand instruments → ultrasonic again for lavage.

hints.quote: Always have a look at x-rays even before you start capturing your numbers.
hints.take: Radiographs show bone loss (localized/generalized, horizontal/vertical), tipping, fused roots, root proximity, calculus, the sinus and PA lesions. Keep them open during SRP rather than the chart.

hints.quote: You are not expected to memorize the numbers. This is just to give you an idea if you have a 6 millimeter pocket how much change you can expect.
hints.take: The deck's expected-reduction figures (a 6 mm pocket becoming 5 or 4.5) are for scale only. Know why pockets shrink, not the table.

hints.quote: We are not going to go in detail about the instruments in this session... You don't have to remember the numbers for now, but later you will have to.
hints.take: Instrument numbers and anatomy get dissected in the upcoming PCD sessions (and the must-pass instrument competency). For now: scaler vs. curette, SG = Gracey, SC = the one universal curette.

hints.quote: This is probably, arguably, one of the most important things that I'll mention to you during this entire presentation. So definitely, definitely know this... Attachment loss that involves the furcation, it dramatically decreases the prognosis of the tooth.
hints.take: From the recorded lecture; he repeated it all through. Once CAL reaches the furcation the prognosis falls, because the area is so hard to instrument and to clean.

hints.quote: These are very, very important numbers to know... this is a study that was done back in the 70s, and we still reference this to this day.
hints.take: Bower's entrance depths from the CEJ. Maxillary first molar: mesiopalatal ~3.6 mm, buccal ~4.2 mm, distopalatal ~4.8 mm. Mandibular first molar: buccal ~2.4 mm, lingual ~2.5 mm. A 4-5 mm probing depth may already mean an exposed furcation.

hints.quote: The maxillary buccal furcation is the most commonly affected furcation, followed by the mesiopalatal and distal palatal furcations. I want you to know that.
hints.take: Maxillary molars are affected more than mandibular; on maxillary molars buccal > mesiopalatal > distopalatal; on mandibular molars the buccal is affected most.

hints.quote: The primary cause of furcation involvement is progressive clinical attachment loss that results from inflammatory periodontal disease. So you're probably going to see that test question probably on every single periodontal exam that you have while you're in dental school, you're definitely going to see it on boards.
hints.take: Plaque-driven periodontitis is the primary cause. CEPs, enamel pearls, overhangs, root form and trunk length are contributing factors.

hints.quote: This next one is big. So definitely know it... definite test question, but by far more important than that, know that for life.
hints.take: Cervical enamel projections: amelogenesis fails to halt before root formation; nothing attaches to enamel, so plaque is funneled into the furcation. ~30% of mandibular vs ~15% of maxillary molars, more on second molars and the buccal.

hints.quote: We actually have a classification for cervical enamel projections, and you need to know these. Stupid, stupid easy. It's just grade 1, 2, and 3.
hints.take: Grade 1: the CEJ dips toward the furcation. Grade 2: approaches but doesn't enter. Grade 3: enters the furcation. No bone or attachment loss: observe. Loss: remove it.

hints.quote: Whenever you see a lone furcation involvement in an otherwise periodontally stable patient... that should prompt you as the clinician to examine for the presence of a cervical enamel projection.
hints.take: One deep site on one tooth means a cause specific to that tooth: a CEP, an overhang, retained cement, a vertical root fracture.

hints.quote: They're often manifested by the presence of what are called furcation arrows, and I do want you to know this. Approximately 30 to 55 percent of grade 2 or grade 3 furcation involvements have this furcation arrow present on the radiograph.
hints.take: An arrow means involvement is highly likely, but no arrow rules nothing out: never the sole diagnostic tool. The Nabers probe is the best way to find a furcation.

hints.quote: Do your clinical examination first, arrive at a diagnosis, then look at your radiographs, use your radiographs to prove your diagnosis.
hints.take: His rule for all of dentistry. Take periapicals and vertical bitewings; clinical exam alone found 3% / 9% of involved maxillary / mandibular molars, combined 65% / 23%.

hints.quote: I'm not going to go through all of these, but this is basically just kind of in a nutshell what we're attempting on doing.
hints.take: Said of the step-by-step regeneration slides: know which patients and furcations are good candidates more than each step. Local antibiotics and resective surgery were left for their own lectures.

hints.quote: This is the most important slide that I have for this presentation, largely because of this last bullet point. If the bone does not follow what that overlying gingival architecture is doing, periodontal pocketing will reoccur.
hints.take: The rationale for osseous surgery: gingiva is scalloped and returns to that shape after surgery, so the bone must be reshaped to follow it, or the pockets come back.

hints.quote: You're going to hear me repeat this next bullet point, ad nauseum. This is what we try and do as periodontists... We're trying to create an environment that the patient can keep clean on a daily basis.
hints.take: The goal of Phase I and of surgery alike: shallow pockets the patient can clean. Surgery cures nothing on its own.

hints.quote: Number one, this is huge. There's not a periodontist on this earth that doesn't know this, and that's ineffective plaque control.
hints.take: Ineffective plaque control is the first contraindication to periodontal surgery, which is why the Phase I re-evaluation checks home care before anyone picks up a scalpel.

hints.quote: In pockets measuring between 3 and 5 millimeters, the chances of failure becomes greater. And then when that pocket depth is over 5 millimeters, the chances of failure dominates.
hints.take: The 1981 root planing study: residual calculus rises with pocket depth, which is the case for surgical access.

hints.quote: The most important thing, really, really thoroughly debride these root surfaces. Again, that's the most important step anytime we're doing this kind of surgery.
hints.take: Root debridement is the key step of any periodontal surgery, resective or regenerative: without clean roots nothing works.

hints.quote: Look what I did with this furcation, though. Really preserve. That is bone that we cannot touch. If we do that, we're dooming this tooth to failure.
hints.take: In osseous surgery around a molar, bone is removed on each root's facial and lingual, never in the furcation.

hints.quote: If you see one isolated area on one tooth, site-specific, something's going on.
hints.take: Repeated in class: one deep site in a stable mouth points to a local cause on that tooth (CEP, overhang, residual cement, or a vertical root fracture, which means extraction).

hints.quote: When you come across the scientific evidence... be cautious of the terms used, success versus survival.
hints.take: Survival = the implant is present and restored (loaded) and can still have biologic or prosthetic complications. Success = no complications at all. Know Albrektsson's criteria: immobile, no radiolucency, no pain/infection/paresthesia/neuropathy, ≤1.5 mm bone loss at 1 year (then <0.2 mm a year).

hints.quote: Implants in health can have pocket depth deeper than three millimeters... always compare to the baseline.
hints.take: There is no 3 mm cutoff for implants: health = no increase in probing depth vs previous exams. Capture the clinical and radiographic baseline.

hints.quote: Implants are allowed or expected to have about two millimeters of bone remodeling once they are put to function... And any further bone loss on top of that crestal remodeling... is termed as pathologic.
hints.take: Physiologic vs pathologic bone loss: ~2 mm of crestal remodeling, plateauing in the first year, is normal (the slides give no number; she did). Beyond it = pathologic = peri-implantitis.

hints.quote: When somebody talks about peri-implantitis and you have not yet seen the patient and you have not yet seen the x-ray of the patient, you should have a picture of true bone loss in your mind.
hints.take: The one difference between mucositis and peri-implantitis is bone loss beyond the initial remodeling. Both have inflammation, bleeding/suppuration and deeper probing.

hints.quote: Supuration is a symptom of active disease... Regardless of whatever your long-term plan is for that tooth or for that implant, whenever you see suppuration, you have to do something.
hints.take: Pus = active disease, at a tooth or an implant: debride (and maybe a local antibiotic). Never 'watch' it. Mucositis is reversible, so treat it too.

hints.quote: If implant body has gained mobility, that means loss of osseointegration... which nobody in this universe can reverse. The only thing left for that implant is to come out.
hints.take: Mobile implant = failed = remove it. First confirm the mobility is in the implant body, not the abutment or crown. Peri-implantitis itself rarely makes an implant mobile.

hints.quote: If somebody has to ask you, what is the primary... how does this disease and pathologic loss of bone start? Your answer should be bacteria, plaque, biofilm.
hints.take: Peri-implant disease is multifactorial, but plaque biofilm is the primary cause; periodontitis and peri-implantitis share pathogens.

hints.quote: That is the link, that is the reason why untreated periodontitis is a contraindication for implant therapy.
hints.take: A patient who lost teeth to periodontitis is a susceptible host carrying the same pathogens. Untreated periodontitis = contraindication; treated, arrested, compliant = implants are fine (her conclusion).

hints.quote: With smoking, for how many number of years they have been smoking plus how much they smoke every day matters. With diabetes... the number of years the patient has been diagnosed with diabetes does not matter.
hints.take: Smoking: dose-response. Diabetes: control (HbA1c, 3-4 months = red cell lifespan) matters, duration doesn't; poorly controlled = contraindicated.

hints.quote: Radiographs when it comes to implant health are not for exploration... But once clinical changes are found, you confirm that on the x-ray.
hints.take: Radiographs are confirmatory, not exploratory: baseline at the final restoration, every 6 months in year 1, then annually, plus when PD, BOP or suppuration change.

hints.quote: Absence of bleeding, very good indication of absence of disease, but presence of bleeding is not that great.
hints.take: BOP: absence predicts stability; presence shows inflammation but not necessarily progression (force, angulation). Bleeding at 4 of 4 visits: 30%; 0 of 4: 1.5%.

hints.quote: The characteristics of peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis... make sure that the key difference between health and implantitis is that bone loss... how to differentiate between physiologic bone loss and pathologic bone loss, and how often should we do risk assessment.
hints.take: Her own end-of-class list of what to know: smoking; mucositis vs peri-implantitis; bone loss as the key difference; physiologic vs pathologic bone loss; and risk assessment at every stage (before placement, during osseointegration, in maintenance, after removal).

hints.quote: This is not part of the lecture or anything. At UAB we use a number as a cutoff, and that is HbA1c of eight or higher than eight is a contraindication.
hints.take: UAB's clinic cutoff (HbA1c ≥8) was an aside, not lecture content. The lecture's point: poorly controlled diabetes contraindicates implants, measured by HbA1c.

hints.quote: Anytime anybody ever asks you, what causes gum disease, what causes periodontal disease? The answer is bacteria and plaque. You find that answer on your multiple choice test question and you circle it, you answer it, and you move on.
hints.take: Bacteria (plaque) are the primary etiologic factor. Smoking and diabetes compound it but can't cause it alone.

hints.quote: This is a huge point, one of the take-home messages from this presentation, and that's the use of systemic or locally delivered antibiotics. It is not to be used as a monotherapy in the treatment of periodontal disease.
hints.take: Antibiotics are always an adjunct to surgical and non-surgical therapy, given after SRP. Indications: acute infection with systemic signs, aggressive and refractory periodontitis.

hints.quote: This next point is huge. And that's biofilms, they're insoluble, making them very, very difficult to remove... at some point you just got to get in there and scrub it off the tooth surface.
hints.take: The dirty-pot analogy: rinses and water piks don't remove biofilm; mechanical debridement does. Biofilms resist antibiotics by a physical barrier, β-lactamase and a slower growth rate.

hints.quote: If we ever prescribe two antibiotics to be given simultaneously, they've got to be both bactericidal agents or both bacteriostatic agents, but not one from each category.
hints.take: Bactericidal drugs only kill dividing bacteria; a bacteriostatic drug stops division. Amoxicillin + metronidazole works because both are bactericidal.

hints.quote: The very next question that you're going to ask somebody whenever they tell you that they have an allergy to something is what kind of reaction do you have when you take it?
hints.take: Upset stomach = side effect. Hives or difficulty breathing = true (anaphylactic) allergy: nothing from that class. 10-15% of adults report a penicillin allergy.

hints.quote: You don't ever change, you don't ever alter, you don't ever take a patient off a medication that another clinician or physician prescribed.
hints.take: Antibiotics (via vitamin K-producing gut flora) and metronidazole raise warfarin's effect. You can prescribe; tell the physician and let them decide.

hints.quote: If they have a true allergic reaction to the penicillins, 10% of patients are going to have a true allergic reaction to the cephalosporins... if they're allergic to cephalosporins, there's 100% chance they're going to be allergic to the penicillins.
hints.take: Penicillin-allergic and unsure about cephalosporins: don't give one. Cephalosporin-allergic: move on to another class. Clindamycin is usually next (not with colitis).

hints.quote: Number one, it can change the color of your urine. Number two, whatever you do, do not drink alcohol or you will hate life.
hints.take: The two things to tell every metronidazole patient: orange-red urine, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.

hints.quote: We got one site that's starting to break down rather than bringing the patient through surgery. It's kind of a last ditch effort.
hints.take: Local delivery's real indication: one site breaking down in a stable maintenance patient, after debriding it. Not a dozen sites (they need surgery) and not aggressive periodontitis.

hints.quote: Due to its high incidence of bacterial resistance, erythromycin in the treatment of periodontal disease just is not recommended.
hints.take: Erythromycin: high resistance and near-universal GI upset. Azithromycin and clarithromycin cover anaerobes better.

hints.quote: Digoxin, this you got to know though... So now you'll always remember that.
hints.take: His Van Gogh story (Starry Night halos = digoxin toxicity) is there to make one interaction stick: macrolides can raise digoxin levels.

hints.quote: It's 4 millimeters high, 4 millimeters wide. You don't need to know these dimensions.
hints.take: PerioChip's dimensions aren't worth memorizing; know its content (2.5 mg chlorhexidine in gelatin), that it's self-retentive and biodegradable, and the 2-hour peak.

hints.quote: Anybody ever ask you what the primary etiological factor of periodontal disease is, it's bacteria. Don't even look at the other answers. It's bacteria. It's plaque.
hints.take: Said again in the Nov 5 class: bacteria (plaque) are the primary etiologic factor. And "definitely know this one": antibiotics alone are not indicated.

hints.quote: This is a big one. Star this one. Know this one for life... The only way to get rid of a biofilm comes with mechanical debridement.
hints.take: Biofilms are insoluble and stuck to the root: rinses and water piks leave them. Antibiotics come only at the completion of Phase I, after debridement.

hints.quote: I definitely would know dosing. Absolutely... I would know this. I would know this for the exam. It's important to know.
hints.take: Know his dosing chart: Augmentin 250-500 mg tid × 10 days; amoxicillin 375 + metronidazole 250 mg tid × 7 days; clindamycin 150-300 mg qid × 10 days; doxycycline 100 mg bid day 1, then 100 mg a day, × 10-14 days; metronidazole 250 mg tid-qid × 10 days; minocycline 200 mg bid day 1, then 100 mg bid, × 10-14 days; tetracycline 250 mg qid × 14-21 days. Metronidazole regimens: not under 16. And the drug slides' doses.

hints.quote: It's not sufficient to induce the clinical signs of attachment loss. And know this last bullet point. It's ultimately the host response to the presence of bacteria that mediates tissue destruction.
hints.take: Gram-negative bacteria are required but not sufficient: the host response to them does most of the damage.

hints.quote: Without the key, the engine isn't going to start, right? But the engine is what gets you from point A to point B.
hints.take: Bacteria are the key; the host response is the engine. Periodontal disease is not an autoimmune disease. Deeper pockets, more bacteria, a bigger response, more breakdown: a vicious cycle.

hints.quote: You know these next two slides, you're going to have a pretty good understanding of the way periodontal disease works.
hints.take: Pellicle within minutes; gram-positive cocci first, then the orange and red complexes. Complement calls in PMNs and releases histamine (edema). Neutrophils first (24-48 h), macrophages later. IL-1 (osteoclast activating factor): osteoclasts, collagenase, PGE2, MMPs.

hints.quote: You better know what you're doing before you start monkeying around with this.
hints.take: Why host modulation goes slowly: turn the host response down too far and an innocent infection could turn lethal.

hints.quote: We give it at 20 milligrams, so a fifth of the dose, 20 milligrams. We give it twice a day.
hints.take: Periostat (sub-antimicrobial doxycycline): 20 mg bid vs the antibiotic's 100 mg once a day. No antimicrobial activity, so no resistance and long-term use; inhibits collagenase from PMNs; the first FDA-approved systemic host modulator, an adjunct to SRP.

hints.quote: What causes this? Trauma.
hints.take: BRONJ: scraping the necrotic bone is trauma, the very cause, so lesions grow. Bisphosphonates stay in the system for years; most complications are with high-dose IV. No bisphosphonate is approved for periodontal disease.

hints.quote: Don't know the specific numbers from this one particular study, just know basically what it's saying here.
hints.take: Caton 2000: SRP + Periostat beat SRP + placebo at 3, 6 and 9 months, statistically significant but by fractions of a millimeter. Know the point (is it clinically significant?), not the numbers.

hints.quote: The key word here is inflammation is what's causing recession to actually happen. And all the lists of factors that I shared with you are mainly predisposing factors that are there to make this happen.
hints.take: Inflammation causes recession, by either pathway (brushing trauma or plaque). Thin phenotype, brushing, dehiscences, orthodontics, margins, the frenum and smokeless tobacco only predispose.

hints.quote: That classification should help you identify those different defects and be able to identify when or not should you propose a soft tissue graft.
hints.take: Cairo: RT1 (no interproximal loss) about 100% coverage; RT2 (interproximal CAL less than or equal to buccal) partial, about 50-60%, up to the interproximal level; RT3 (interproximal greater) none.

hints.quote: If you do a graft to achieve root coverage for recession type 3, you would not end up achieving that root coverage at all.
hints.take: RT3 is the one type not to graft for root coverage; the other types should be considered for treatment when indicated.

hints.quote: They found that those recessions do progress over time if left untreated.
hints.take: Chambrone and Tatakis (2016): untreated recession progresses, so a recession that doesn't hurt still needs a decision.

hints.quote: If your goal is to cover your graft with a flap, we want it to be only connective tissue graft. We don't want to put epithelium underneath the inner layer of the flap.
hints.take: Covered graft = CTG (connective tissue only). Exposed graft = FGG (epithelium plus lamina propria).

hints.quote: We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft.
hints.take: Root coverage with a CTG or an ADM: the flap is advanced coronally, tension free, over the graft.

hints.quote: It's more or less like a band-aid. Therefore whenever we use these products we do our best to fully cover those grafts.
hints.take: An acellular dermal matrix has no cells or blood supply: always fully covered; remodeled and replaced by the patient's tissue; best for many teeth at once.

hints.quote: Those patients who have less than two millimeters of keratinized gingiva are likely prone to developing recession... but it is a case by case.
hints.take: With good plaque control KG isn't essential; with suboptimal plaque control at least 2 mm is needed to prevent attachment loss.

hints.quote: If I covered it with the flap, then I would deny it the ability to go ahead and turn into keratinized tissue.
hints.take: To create KG, use an FGG left exposed with an apically positioned flap. A CTG covered by mucosa gains no KG.

hints.quote: With thinner phenotype we can expect to have a predisposition for having soft tissue recession as opposed to thicker phenotypes which tend to be more resistant.
hints.take: Probe visible through the tissue = thin (1 mm or less), prone to recession; not visible = thick (more than 1 mm).

hints.quote: Toothbrushing seems to be the most common one.
hints.take: Of the traumatic factors (brushing, flossing, habits, foreign objects, caustic medicaments), toothbrushing is the most common.

hints.quote: There are different ways to treat recessions that may be restorative, but we'll talk about that in next year's course.
hints.take: Restorative treatment of recession is next year's course; this session tests soft tissue grafting.

diagnosis-tx-planning: CAL = PD + GR (signed). Confirm attachment AND bone loss before staging off probing depth alone
RT1 no interproximal loss / RT2 buccal > interproximal / RT3 interproximal > buccal
Stage 1-2: CAL ≤4 mm, coronal third. Stage 3-4: CAL ≥5 mm, middle third or beyond, separated by tooth loss (≤4 vs ≥5) and complexity, not by more CAL
Auto Stage 3/4: vertical loss ≥3 mm, Class II-III furcation, tooth loss to periodontitis
Default Grade B; ratio >1 → C. Heavy smoking or HbA1c ≥7% force Grade C regardless of ratio
More remaining bony walls = better regeneration prognosis (3-wall best, 1-wall worst)
Phase I always first; caries control is part of Phase I; the final crown or RPD waits until perio therapy is done
Maintenance is not a prophylaxis: treated-but-unmaintained patients lose teeth ~2x faster
incisions-flaps-sutures: Intrasulcular = crestal: same incision, named by whether a tooth is present
Sulcular flap (no vertical) → pyramidal (1 vertical) → trapezoidal (2 verticals) as access needs grow
Envelope/pouch flap = buccal only, papillae untouched: the root-coverage design
Sub-marginal incision = excisional, below the free margin, for pocket elimination; creates recession on purpose
Full thickness whenever bone is the goal (implant, augmentation, crown lengthening); split thickness only for soft-tissue grafts
Resorbable: chromic gut (fastest, worst handling) < PGCL < PGA (slowest, best handling, worst reaction)
Non-resorbable: polypropylene (like nylon) / silk (worst reaction, remove at 7 d) / PTFE (priciest, broadest use)
Monofilament beats braided (braided wicks bacteria); wipe braided sutures with CHX before removal
Palatal CTG harvest: molar area (more lamina propria, less fat that would shrink)
Horizontal mattress = augmentation workhorse, but strangles blood supply if overtightened
Vertical mattress = esthetic-zone papillae, oro-antral closure
Continuous/locking = fast seal, whole-line failure risk; long edentulous spans
Flap base at least as wide as its free edge
Vertical incisions at the line angle, never mid-papilla or mid-facial (both confirmed quiz questions)
risk-assessment: McGuire & Nunn sorts by maintainability: Good → Fair → Poor → Questionable → Hopeless (don't swap poor and questionable)
M&N is ~80% right overall, ~50% once good teeth are excluded; teeth usually outlast the prediction
Only M&N can be diagnostic (no-treatment outcome); all three systems can be therapeutic
Kwok & Caton: can stability be achieved with treatment? Questionable sits in the middle; best for medically complex patients
Miller & McEntire: molars only, quantitative, therapeutic; smokers ~296% more likely to lose molars
Regenerating a stage-defining vertical defect or furcation is the only way back from Stage 3
~70% of molar-incisor-pattern teens have a neutrophil chemotactic deficiency; ~70% who generalize use nicotine
~10% resistant · 10-15% at risk for severe disease · 20-25% don't respond to standard therapy
P4/P5 medicine = Personalized, Preventive, Predictive, Participatory (+ Periodontal)
72% of periodontitis patients first present just wanting a cleaning; the D1110 share rises with age
PISA: healthy ≈34 mm² vs. mild-moderate periodontitis ≈2,309 mm²
Low risk: exam 6-12 mo, biofilm removal 6 mo. Moderate: screening 6 mo, debridement 4-6 mo. High: screening 3 mo, debridement 2-4 mo
Recolonization takes 9-11 weeks → 3-month recall; ortho patients 4-6 weeks
#1 reason patients decline treatment is lack of trust, not cost
phase1-therapy: Flagged "on the quiz": plaque bacteria initiate, the host drives progression; bacteria ~25% of damage, host ~75% (cytokines, osteoclasts); bacteria bring LPS
Three diagnoses: health / gingivitis / periodontitis. Periodontitis can never be on an intact periodontium
Plaque (probe 1 mm in, or disclosing tab) and BOP are scored 1/0, presence only. Delayed bleeding = 1
Smoking masks inflammation (cyanotic); diabetes exaggerates it; amlodipine → bulbous interdental overgrowth
In health PD ≠ CAL. CAL = PD + GR with sign: PD 5, GR −3 → CAL 2. Blank or 0 in Salud → CAL = PD → over-diagnosis
Negative GR: probe to base, withdraw until you feel the CEJ. Harder with inflammation, overgrowth, altered passive eruption, calculus/margins
Interproximal probing goes under the contact, not at the line angle. 6 sites per tooth
Debridement: not therapeutic, never with SRP, only when you can't see the margin, full-mouth code only, exam ~2 wk later (combinable at school)
Glickman: I catch (no tx) · II cul-de-sac (best for regeneration) · III through-and-through (hardest) · IV visible (root caries → hopeless)
Rolling technique finds the MGJ / keratinized width (teeth and implants)
Mobility: two blunt instruments; depressible = extract. Fremitus = mobility in function, palpated not seen
Occlusal findings go in the notes section. Pocket tx won't fix grade 2 mobility without fixing the occlusion
Look at x-rays before SRP, not the chart: bone loss pattern, tipping, fused roots, root proximity, calculus, sinus, PA lesion
SRP goals: less inflammation, gram− → gram+, arrest progression. Does not reverse damage; pocket elimination is not the rationale
PD drops from more recession (edema resolves) + reattachment: JE 7-10 d, CT 4-6 wk, collagen 3-6 mo. Re-eval 4-6 wk (deck: DGJ 2-4 wk, maturation 9-12 mo)
Scaling = supra + sub; root planing = sub, roots only; done together
Prophy = never had periodontitis; maintenance = treated periodontitis (localized SRP allowed); D4346 = between them, no periodontitis
Re-eval: residual calculus → remove, re-eval in 2 wk; otherwise more SRP won't help, better OH will
(Not on midterm) Piezo can go sub-G but can't root plane: ultrasonic → hand → ultrasonic lavage
(Not on midterm) Scalers: 2 cutting edges, short powerful strokes, sub-G only ~1-3 mm. Curettes: longer lighter strokes; Gracey (SG) 1 edge; the one SC = universal
One vs. multiple sessions and hand vs. ultrasonic: no difference; irrigation adds nothing; PD ≥5 mm → inadequate ~65%
(Not on midterm) Gracey 3/4 anterior · 11/12 and 15/16 mesial posterior · 13/14 distal posterior; Gracey 70° blade, work at 70-80°
(Not on midterm) Polishing (deck): 30 s pumice ≈ 4 µm enamel; low-abrasion, slow, 90°, light and intermittent
resective-furcation: Furcation = normal anatomy; furcation DEFECT = disease there. CAL into the furcation dramatically lowers the prognosis (his #1 point)
Root trunk = CEJ to first divergence, ~30% of attachment. Short trunk: involved early. Long trunk: protective, but short roots and poor resection candidate once involved
Entrances from the CEJ (Bower): max 1st molar M ~3.6, B ~4.2, D ~4.8 mm; mand 1st molar B ~2.4, L ~2.5 mm. Max buccal entrance narrowest; 1st molar trunk shorter than 2nd
Max premolars: ~40% two roots, entrance ~8 mm; mesial depression on the first premolar 100%
81% of entrances <1 mm, 58% <0.75 mm; curette face 0.75-1.10 mm. Mand mesial root 0.7 mm depression 100%; max MB 0.3 mm 94%
Most affected: maxillary > mandibular molars; max buccal > mesiopalatal > distopalatal; mand buccal
Primary cause = CAL from inflammatory periodontal disease (plaque). Contributing: trunk length, root form, close/fused roots, CEP, enamel pearl, overhang, intermediate bifurcation ridge
CEP: amelogenesis fails to stop; no attachment to enamel. Mand ~30%, max ~15%; 2nd molars, buccal. Grade 1 dips, 2 approaches, 3 enters. No loss: observe; loss: remove (warn of thermal sensitivity)
Lone furcation in a stable mouth → look for a CEP
Glickman I feel / II hook + catch / III through / IV through + visible. Hamp 1 <3 mm, 2 >3 mm, 3 through. Tarnow & Fletcher vertical A 0-3, B 4-6, C ≥7
Mesiopalatal: probe from palatal; distopalatal: either side. Palatal root masks max buccal furcation on x-ray. Furcation arrow in 30-55% of II-III; never the sole tool
Clinical exam first, x-rays confirm. Clinical alone 3% / 9%; combined 65% max / 23% mand
Presence alone ≠ treat. Early: no therapy unless an alterable local factor. Goal: minimize or eliminate the furcation
Class I: SRP, local factors, plasty. II: plasty, GTR, resection, extraction. III: tunnel, resection, extraction
Regeneration best: mand + buccal max degree II. Interproximal max II poor (access); degree III = conventional surgery. No smokers / uncontrolled diabetics / poor hygiene. 4 weeks no brushing the site
Tunnel = a Glickman IV on purpose; mand molars with long, divergent roots; caries common

Root resection: most often max 1st molar DB root; commits to endo + restorative. Hemisection: root + crown portion, mand molars. Sequence: endo → provisional → resection → perio surgery (margins ≥3 mm above crest) → final
Resective osseous surgery (in class, not yet lectured): reverse/negative architecture = interdental bone apical to facial/lingual = the target
Resective: if bone doesn't follow the scalloped gingiva, pockets recur (his most important slide)
Re-eval at 4-6 weeks: shallow + clean = maintenance; plaque everywhere = repeat Phase I; clean but deep = surgery
SRP: 3-5 mm failure more likely, >5 mm failure dominates. Ineffective plaque control = contraindication #1
Ostectomy removes supporting bone; osteoplasty reshapes non-supporting bone. ~0.6 mm lost; mobility normal by ~1 year
Steps: vertical grooving, radicular blending, flatten interproximal, gradualize marginal. Never touch furcation bone
periodontal-regeneration: Regeneration = new bone + new cementum + new PDL over a pathologically exposed root. Long junctional epithelium = repair
Four factors: cells, scaffolds, growth factors, blood supply
Best candidate: >3 mm deep, radiographic angle ≤25°, more walls (3-wall best). Deeper + narrower + more walls = more CAL and bone gain
Non-supportive (1-wall) anatomy = failure risk. 1-wall + thin scalloped biotype = more midfacial recession
Toolbox: bone grafts (DFDBA = allograft), GTR membrane, combination (graft holds the space), EMD, PDGF, MIST
EMD = amelogenins, outcomes ~ GTR. rhPDGF-BB = chemotactic/mitogenic/angiogenic. β-TCP = osteoconductive scaffold

Decision tree: fix the patient first (systemic, tobacco, hygiene). <3 mm defect: no regeneration. 3-wall/circumferential <2 mm wide: graft, membrane or biologic. Wide or 2-wall: reinforced membrane, graft + membrane or graft + biologic. 1-wall: combination. High esthetic risk: avoid the membrane
Risk assessment: smoking ≤10/day medium, >10 high; FMPS ≤15% low, ≥25% high; contained = 1-2 sides of the root
OFD baseline: PD ~7 → 4 mm, CAL gain ~1.5 mm, bone gain ~1 mm (rest is recession)
Only histology proves regeneration; subtraction radiography shows change between two standardized films
implants-perio: Survival = present and loaded (complications allowed); success = no complications
Albrektsson 1986: immobile, no radiolucency, no pain/infection/paresthesia, ≤1.5 mm bone loss at 1 year; then <0.2 mm a year
Health: no BOP/suppuration on gentle probing, no PD increase vs previous exams (no 3 mm cutoff), no bone loss beyond remodeling
~2 mm crestal remodeling in year 1 = physiologic; beyond it = pathologic
Mucositis = gingivitis of implants: profuse bleeding/suppuration, deeper PD from swelling, no bone loss, reversible
Peri-implantitis = plaque-associated inflammation + progressive bone loss beyond remodeling. No decontamination method is superior
Meffert: ailing (static, monitor) / failing (progressive + inflamed, not mobile) / failed (mobile: remove; osseointegration can't be regained)
Primary cause: plaque biofilm. Pre-implant flora decides peri-implant flora; pellicle in 30 min; pathogens persist a year after extractions
Untreated periodontitis = contraindication; treated, arrested, compliant = OK. Treat perio first, no immediate implants during disease control
Smoking: 11.3% vs 4.76% failure (Bain & Moy), dose-response (Alsaadi), peri-implantitis 23.5% vs 16.5% (Simonis). Diabetes: HbA1c, not duration
Risk assessment: before placement, during osseointegration, in maintenance, after removal
BOP at ~0.25 N: absence = stability; 4/4 visits 30% → 0/4 1.5%. Radiographs: baseline at the final restoration, 6-monthly in year 1, then yearly; confirmatory, not exploratory
antibiotics-host-mod: Bacteria and plaque cause it; antibiotics only for acute infection with systemic signs, aggressive and refractory periodontitis
Never monotherapy: always an adjunct, given after SRP
Biofilm: barrier, β-lactamase, slow growth; survives 500-1000× systemic levels; must be scrubbed off
Bactericidal needs dividing cells: never pair static + cidal (amoxicillin + metronidazole = both cidal)
Amoxicillin 500 mg po tid × 7 = 21 tabs; cell wall; β-lactamase-sensitive. Augmentin adds clavulanate (125 mg), more GI upset and cost
True allergy = hives or trouble breathing. PCN-allergic and unsure about cephalosporins: no cephalosporin (10% cross). Next: clindamycin (not with colitis: C. diff)
Tetracycline: 30S, static, A.a., no dairy/antacids, stains (<8 y, pregnancy), sun. Doxy 100 qd, mino 100 bid
Macrolides: 50S, static; erythromycin not recommended; Z-Pak 500 then 250 × 4, away from food; clarithromycin pregnancy C; raise digoxin
Metronidazole: obligate anaerobes, DNA, cidal; ANUG; orange-red urine, no alcohol; raises warfarin. Cipro: DNA gyrase, anaerobes resistant, 1 h before / 2 h after meals, with metronidazole
Warfarin: prescribe, but tell the physician. All antibiotics: weaker oral contraceptives, C. diff, GI upset (yogurt, Diflucan)

Local delivery after SRP, for one breaking-down site in a stable maintenance patient: PerioChip 2.5 mg CHX (peak 2 h), Atridox 10% doxy (7 days no brushing/flossing/eating), Arestin 1 mg mino (14 days; no brushing 12 h, no flossing 10 days)

Know the dosing chart: Augmentin 250-500 tid × 10 d; amox 375 + metro 250 tid × 7 d (not under 16); clinda 150-300 qid × 10 d; doxy 100 bid day 1 then 100/day × 10-14 d; metro 250 tid-qid × 10 d; mino 200 bid day 1 then 100 bid × 10-14 d; tetracycline 250 qid × 14-21 d
Bacteria = the key, host response = the engine: required, not sufficient; not autoimmune; vicious cycle
Complement calls PMNs + histamine (edema); neutrophils 24-48 h, then macrophages; IL-1 = osteoclast activating factor → osteoclasts, collagenase, PGE2, MMPs

NSAIDs block PGE2 (daily for years; GI, bleeding). Bisphosphonates: BRONJ (scraping = trauma = cause; high-dose IV), none approved. Periostat 20 mg bid (a fifth of 100 mg) inhibits collagenase, no resistance; small gains (Caton 2000). Step lightly
perio-plastic-esthetics: Recession: a thin phenotype (1 mm or less, the probe shows through) is predisposed; the key word is inflammation, from brushing trauma or plaque
Cairo: RT1 (no interproximal loss) ~100% coverage; RT2 (interproximal loss less than buccal) partial; RT3 (more than buccal) don't graft for coverage
Covered by a flap = CTG only (no epithelium), under a coronally advanced flap. Left exposed = FGG, which creates keratinized gingiva
ADM = the most common allograft: no donor site, many teeth at once, must be fully covered; not as good as an autograft in demanding sites
Keratinized gingiva isn't essential with good plaque control; under 2 mm with poor plaque control is at risk. Untreated recession progresses
Palate: greater palatine artery ~7 / 12 / 17 mm from the CEJ in a shallow / average / high vault
APE: Type 1A = gingivectomy; Type 2A = apically positioned flap; both B = flap + osseous surgery
Upper lip 20-22 mm (F), 22-24 mm (M), mobility 6-8 mm; lateral margin 1 mm coronal; golden proportion 1.618 : 1 : 0.618

sections.title: The four-step staging workflow
sections.html:
StepWhat you do
1. Initial screeningReview full-mouth radiographs, full-mouth probing depths, and missing teeth to sort the case into mild-to-moderate (Stage 1–2) vs. severe-to-very-severe (Stage 3–4).
2. Fine-tune the stageDetermine maximum CAL/RBL, confirm horizontal vs. vertical bone loss, assess periodontitis-related tooth loss, and weigh case complexity (probing depth, furcation, occlusion, need for multidisciplinary treatment).
3. Determine the gradeWeigh history/risk relative to age, risk-factor control, systemic health, response to initial therapy, and compliance. Default to Grade B and look for evidence to move to A or C.
4. Build the treatment planStage 1–2 (any grade) → standard periodontal treatment. Stage 3–4 → complex and/or multidisciplinary treatment.

sections.title: Intrabony defect wall configurations
sections.html:
ConfigurationWhat it means
1-wall defectOnly one bony wall remains around the root (commonly just the wall against the neighboring tooth). Worst prognosis for regeneration.
2-wall defectTwo bony walls remain. When bone is lost on both neighboring root surfaces and only the buccal and lingual walls remain, this specific 2-wall pattern is called a crater.
3-wall defectThree bony walls remain (buccal, lingual, and the wall against the neighboring tooth) — only the involved root surface itself lacks bone. Best prognosis for bone regeneration; more remaining walls means a better case for regrowing bone.

sections.title: Suturing techniques
sections.html:
TechniqueNotes
Single InterruptedEach throw tied and cut independently — the general-purpose default. Figure-8 is a common variant.
Criss-CrossCrossed throws over the site; named alongside interrupted techniques in the course slides.
Horizontal MattressLayered closure and bone-augmentation cases; essential for larger augmentations; prevents flap-margin inversion; needs high tensile strength. Overtightening constricts blood supply to the incision edge → risk of bone necrosis and dehiscence.
Vertical MattressInternal mattress for maximal tissue approximation and eversion; approximates papillae in the esthetic zone; usable to close oro-antral communications.
Continuous / Continuous LockingBites sit close together for a better seal; monofilament or high-glide material risks the whole line coming undone if one throw fails. Used for edentulous long-span areas, alveoloplasties, apicoectomies.
SlingWraps around a single tooth to reposition the flap/papilla without engaging the opposing side.
Periosteal AnchorageAnchors the flap to periosteum for controlled apical or lateral repositioning.

sections.title: Incision types
sections.html:
IncisionNotes
Intrasulcular incisionBlade inserted in the sulcus around a present tooth, separating the gingival fibers from the tooth — runs around the full circumference: buccal, lingual, and through the papillae. This is the same physical incision as a "crestal" incision; it only gets the intrasulcular name because a tooth is there.
Crestal incisionThe identical straight incision along the ridge, used instead of "intrasulcular" only because the site is edentulous — there is no sulcus to speak of. Naming is about tooth presence, not technique.
Vertical (releasing) incisionPlaced vertically at the line angle of a tooth to open a bigger flap than intrasulcular/crestal incisions alone can give — dropped whenever the surgery (soft-tissue, bone, or sinus augmentation) needs more apical exposure than a small flap provides. One vertical makes a pyramidal flap; two make a trapezoidal flap.
Sub-marginal incisionPlaced below (not at) the free gingival margin, scalloped through the pocket wall — excisional rather than reflect-and-reposition, used specifically to eliminate a periodontal pocket in resective/osseous surgery (e.g. trimming ~3 mm off a 6 mm pocket to leave a shallow, cleansable sulcus). Creates recession by design; never used on a site being treated for recession instead.

sections.title: Flap designs
sections.html:
Flaps are also classified by: Bone exposure after flap reflection (full-thickness vs. split-thickness); Placement of the flap after surgery (coronal to CEJ for soft-tissue augmentation vs. apical for crown lengthening / osseous surgery); Management of the papillae (papilla-sparing or not).

DesignNotes
Sulcular flapIntrasulcular incision around the surgical tooth plus one adjacent tooth on each side, no vertical release. Limited access and hard to advance because the tissue stays attached laterally — the first option for minor augmentation or single implant placement. Extending it to include more teeth (still no vertical) buys moderate additional access without dropping a vertical incision.
Pyramidal flapOne vertical incision plus an intrasulcular incision across three teeth (e.g. distal of #7, then intrasulcular on 7-8-9) — named for the triangular shape it opens. Used when a periapical lesion or graft site needs more exposure than a sulcular flap gives but doesn't justify releasing both sides — a classic choice for implant placement with an onlay graft.
Trapezoidal flapTwo vertical incisions, one on each side of the defect, combined with the intrasulcular incision between them. Needed for major augmentation (vertical ridge grafts, large sinus lifts) because two releases let the flap coronally advance with passive, tension-free closure over the graft — a single vertical often can't stretch that far without tearing.
Envelope (pouch) flapBuccal-only elevation with no papilla reflection at all — the papillae are left completely intact. Used for soft-tissue augmentation (root coverage) where the graft needs to be tucked under coronally advanced tissue without disturbing the interdental architecture.
Full-thickness (mucoperiosteal) flapPeriosteum reflected with the flap; exposes bone.
Split-thickness flapPeriosteum left on the bone; only mucosa/submucosa reflected — used when apical repositioning or periosteal preservation is needed.
Papilla-sparing flapKeeps the interdental papilla intact — favored for esthetic and regenerative surgery.

Five surgical principles: Perform the incision with a firm, continuous stroke. · The incision must be at a distance from the lesion or bony defect, not directly over it. · Vertical incisions are made at the line angle of the tooth. · Periosteum must be reflected as an integral part of the flap. · The base of the flap must be as wide as the free edge of the flap, to protect its blood supply.

sections.title: Radiograph reads and SRP limitations
sections.html:
What the x-ray tells you before you probe

  • Localized vs. generalized
  • Horizontal vs. vertical (or both)
  • Tipped teeth
  • Fused roots
  • Root proximity
  • Calculus (the cause, and removable)
  • Sinus proximity
  • Periapical lesions

Limitations of SRP (as taught)

  • Pocket depth and access
  • A blinded, tactile procedure
  • Motile bacteria invading the pocket lining
  • Restorative margins: overhanging, subgingival, open, rough
  • Furcations
  • Developmental grooves, fissures, concavities
  • Over-removing cementum → hypersensitivity
  • Patient compliance with hygiene
  • Operator skill (a learning curve)

sections.title: What the evidence says
sections.html:
QuestionFinding
Single vs. multiple sessionsNo considerable advantage to multiple sessions. Calculus left after several sessions stays for the same reasons it stays after one (Anderson et al. 1996).
Manual vs. mechanically drivenNo statistical difference in PD reduction or CAL gain.
Adding subgingival irrigationChlorhexidine, saline, or peroxide irrigation with ultrasonic instrumentation added no improvement.
Limits of non-surgical therapyRoot debridement is inadequate about 65% of the time in PD ≥5 mm. It is not 100% effective against A. actinomycetemcomitans. Overhanging restorations, furcations, and root anatomy get in the way. Removing cementum can cause hypersensitivity. Results depend on operator skill and on compliance with hygiene and maintenance (Greenstein 2000).

sections.title: Phase I evaluation (re-evaluation)

ItemDetail
When4-6 weeks after Phase I therapy
What to recordPlaque scores, signs of gingival inflammation, BOP, PD, recession, CAL, mobility, furcation, suppuration
Healing timelineLargest PD changes in the first 4 weeks, mostly from resolving inflammation and edema (and the recession that follows). Dentogingival junction re-established at 2-4 weeks. Repair and maturation continue for 9-12 months.
If therapy failedAssess tissue response, remaining deposits, health history and risk factors, and consider a plaque culture. Then: antibiotics/antimicrobials, host modulation, repeat non-surgical therapy, re-evaluate, or move to Phase II surgery.

sections.title: To polish or not to polish
sections.html:
For

  • Removes extrinsic stain that brushing and scaling leave behind
  • Prepares teeth for caries-preventive agents (sealants, fluoride gels and varnishes)
  • Patient satisfaction

Against

  • 30 s with pumice can remove up to 4 µm of enamel, and the outermost layer holds the most fluoride
  • A coarse abrasive can leave the surface rougher than before
  • Steady pressure from a fast rubber cup can cause pain and possible pulpal damage
  • A rubber cup with pumice for 2 min can completely remove the sulcular epithelium
  • Pumice can be pushed subgingivally

Technique: Low-abrasion paste, slow-speed handpiece, minimal heat, rubber cup at 90° to the tooth with intermittent light pressure.

sections.html:
TermMeaning
FurcationNormal anatomical region of a multi-rooted tooth where the roots diverge from the root trunk
Furcation defectDestruction of soft tissue and bone in the furcation from periodontal infection; dramatically lowers the prognosis

sections.title: Furcation anatomy
sections.html:
Maxillary first molar (as taught, Bower 1979)

  • Three entrances, from the CEJ: mesiopalatal ~3.6 mm, buccal ~4.2 mm, distopalatal ~4.8 mm (another slide: ~3.5 / 4 / 5 mm; the exam-review guide: 3 / 3.5 / 5 mm)
  • The straight buccal entrance is generally the narrowest (the two buccal roots sit close)
  • The first molar has a shorter root trunk than the second molar
  • Probe the mesiopalatal from the palatal (it is offset palatally); the distopalatal from either side

Mandibular first molar

  • Two entrances, from the CEJ: buccal ~2.4 mm, lingual ~2.5 mm, much shallower than maxillary
  • Lingual angulation puts the lingual entrance a little more apical (a slide also gives it as >4 mm and >0.75 mm wide)
  • Mesial root wider buccolingually: hourglass or kidney-bean cross-section

Maxillary premolars

  • ~40% have two roots
  • Mean furcation entrance ~8 mm from the CEJ: long trunk, short roots
  • Maxillary first premolar: a ~0.5 mm mesial developmental depression next to the furcation, present 100% of the time (floss misses it)

Width vs. your instruments

  • 81% of furcation entrances are <1 mm wide; 58% are <0.75 mm
  • A curette blade face is 0.75-1.10 mm wide, so most entrances are narrower than the blade

sections.title: Cervical enamel projections
sections.html:
GradeWhat it isUsual management
Grade 1Distinct change in the CEJ pointing apically toward the furcationUsually observe if no bone or attachment loss
Grade 2Approaches the furcation but does not enter itUsually observe if no bone or attachment loss
Grade 3Extends into the furcationRemove when bone or attachment loss is associated
  • Forms when amelogenesis fails to halt before root formation: a narrow wedge of enamel from the CEJ toward the furcation
  • New attachment will NOT form on enamel
  • Mandibular molars ~30%, maxillary molars ~15%; more on second molars and on the buccal
  • Thin: remove with a diamond or finishing bur. Thick: attempt with care not to expose the pulp; warn of thermal sensitivity on a vital tooth
  • A lone furcation involvement in an otherwise stable patient: look for a CEP

sections.title: Furcation classifications: Glickman, Hamp, Tarnow & Fletcher
sections.html:
SystemGradesMeasures
Glickman (1953)I: probe into the flute, interradicular bone intact (incipient). II: bone lost, not through. III: through-and-through. IV: through-and-through with recession (visible)Horizontal, by probe feel (Nabers probe)
Hamp (1975)Degree 1: <3 mm horizontal. Degree 2: >3 mm, not through. Degree 3: through-and-throughHorizontal, in mm
Tarnow & Fletcher (1984)Subclass A: 0-3 mm. B: 4-6 mm. C: ≥7 mmVertical, in mm (a subclass added to the above)

Finding furcations

  • Nabers probe: the best way to find a furcation (clinical exam first, radiographs confirm)
  • Easy to reach: maxillary buccal; mandibular buccal and lingual
  • Mesiopalatal (maxillary): probe from the palatal. Distopalatal: from either side
  • Maxillary buccal furcation bone loss is often masked by the superimposed palatal root
  • Furcation arrows mark mesiopalatal/distopalatal lesions; seen in ~30-55% of Grade II-III; present = highly likely, absent ≠ ruled out; never the sole tool
  • Take periapicals AND vertical bitewings
  • Ross & Thompson 1980: clinical exam alone found 3% (maxillary) / 9% (mandibular); combined 65% / 23%

sections.html:

Class IIFurcation plasty, regeneration (GTR), root resection, extraction
Class IIITunnel preparation, root resection, tooth extraction
ApproachTypeWhenNote
SRP (Phase I)Non-surgicalEvery case; plaque-free root surfaces come firstCurette face 0.75-1.10 mm vs most entrances <1 mm

Regeneration (additive)SurgicalBest: mandibular and buccal maxillary degree IIInterproximal maxillary II much less suited; degree III no better than conventional surgery
TunnelSurgicalDeep Class II and III; mandibular molars with long, divergent rootsCreates a Glickman IV on purpose; caries is common

HemisectionSurgicalMandibular molarsRoot + its part of the crown; makes a single-rooted tooth; rarer since implants

Regeneration: who and how

  • Patient: not with uncontrolled diabetes, immunocompromise, smoking, poor compliance or poor hygiene
  • Best teeth: mandibular and buccal maxillary degree II furcations
  • Interproximal maxillary degree II: significantly less suited (limited access)
  • Degree III: no difference from conventional surgery
  • In favor: thicker biotype, no recession, coronal interproximal bone. Root proximity may impair it; a root canal filling is not a contraindication
  • Steps: sulcular incision + full-thickness flap → clean the roots → remove enamel projections/pearls → bone graft and/or GTR membrane → membrane held by a resorbable sling suture → flap secured coronally
  • After: no mechanical plaque removal at the site for up to 4 weeks (chlorhexidine instead); judge by radiographic bone fill at ~1 year

Root separation/resection sequence

  • Endodontic treatment, access filled directly with amalgam or composite
  • Provisional restoration
  • Root separation and resection: don't expose the interradicular bone, leave fornix behind, perforate the canals, or leave sharp angles
  • Periodontal surgery: remove bone defects around the remaining roots; provisional margins ≥3 mm coronal to the bone crest
  • Final restoration: rigid framework; occlusion that minimizes lateral forces

sections.title: Resective osseous surgery
sections.html:
PointDetail
SRP limits (1981)Residual calculus rises with pocket depth: 3-5 mm failure more likely; >5 mm failure dominates (more surface, more irregularities, narrow apical portion)
Why osseous surgeryGingiva is scalloped and reverts to it even if bone does not; if bone does not follow the gingiva, pockets recur
OchsenbeinEliminate bony deformities so bone and gingiva are consistent and the pocket is reduced or eliminated
Healthy crest on a radiographAbout 1-2 mm from the adjacent CEJs
Bone lostAbout 0.6 mm of supporting bone height around the tooth; removed facially and lingually, interproximal bone preserved
MobilityIncreases after osseous resection; returns to pre-op levels after about 1 year (Selipsky 1976)
FurcationsTreat each buccal root of a maxillary molar like its own tooth; never remove the bone in the furcation
Most important stepThorough root debridement: without clean roots nothing works

Indications

  • Active periodontitis that Phase I failed to eradicate
  • Moderate to severe PD with limited improvement after SRP (slides: >4 mm and furcations; in class: about 5 mm and deeper)
  • Mild to moderate horizontal bone loss
  • 2-wall crater defects; shallow 1-, 2- and 3-wall defects
  • Better access to shallow furcation defects
  • Remove ledges and exostoses (buccal exostoses, lingual tori)
  • Create positive osseous architecture

Contraindications

  • Ineffective plaque control (the big one)
  • Noncompliance with the treatment plan (e.g., wants to skip Phase I)
  • Shallow pocket depths (surgery causes attachment loss)
  • Hard-tissue defect amenable to regeneration
  • Anticipated unacceptable cosmetic result (e.g., maxillary anteriors, high smile line)
  • Uncontrolled systemic disease
TermMeaning
OstectomyRemoval of tooth-supporting bone (alveolar bone proper, part of the attachment apparatus) to reach a more physiologic form
OsteoplastyReshaping the alveolar process without removing supporting bone (no attachment to the tooth); can be more aggressive

Steps

  • 1. Vertical grooving (interproximal; osteoplasty; large round burs)
  • 2. Radicular blending
  • 3. Flattening interproximal bone
  • 4. Gradualizing marginal bone (conservative ostectomy, facial and lingual)

sections.title: Bone architecture: positive, flat, reverse
sections.html:
ArchitecturePattern
PositiveInterdental bone sits coronal to its midfacial/midlingual margins; radicular bone is apical to interdental bone. The normal, healthy pattern.
FlatInterdental and radicular bone sit at roughly the same level.
Reverse (negative)Interdental bone sits apical to its midfacial/midlingual margins — apical to radicular bone. Creates osseous craters and deep interproximal pockets; resective surgery aims to restore positive architecture (or flat when that would cost too much bone).

sections.title: Regeneration: definition and case selection
sections.html:
• Regeneration = new bone, new cementum and new PDL, a new functional attachment apparatus over a pathologically exposed root (1996 World Workshop). Healing without it (e.g., long junctional epithelium) is repair
  • Factors: cells, scaffolds, growth factors and blood supply. Strategies: tissue engineering (bring cells in) vs endogenous regeneration (cell-free: recruit the host's own cells)
  • Intrabony defects are classified by number of walls, width and depth
  • Depth >3 mm and radiographic defect angle ≤25°: most amenable to conventional GTR
  • Deeper, narrower defects with more walls: more CAL gain and radiographic bone gain at 12 months (Nibali, 2021)
  • Non-supportive anatomy (predominantly 1-wall) is a risk factor for failure (OR ≥10.4)
  • 1-wall vs 2-wall defect (OR 58.8) and thin, scalloped biotype (OR 76.9): risk factors for more midfacial recession (Cosyn, 2012)
  • Nibali 2021 pooled: <4 mm deep about 0.75 mm less bone gain; angle <37° about 0.94 mm more; 1-wall vs 3-wall about 1.2 mm less. Depth had the strongest evidence
  • Walls are confirmed at surgery, after the flap is raised and the defect debrided; a radiograph is 2-D
  • Patient factors that rule regeneration out (Session 5): uncontrolled diabetes, immunocompromise, smoking, poor compliance, poor hygiene

Success criteria: Immobile; No peri-implant radiolucency; No pain, infection, paresthesia, or neuropathy; ≤1.5 mm vertical bone loss at 1 year in function (Albrektsson 1986); In class: <0.2 mm vertical bone loss a year after the first year.

  • Primary cause: plaque biofilm (multifactorial; poor plaque control OR 14.3, Ferreira 2006)
  • Flora before implantation determines the peri-implant flora
  • Stable implants: flora resembles a healthy dentate patient's subgingival flora
  • Pellicle forms ~30 minutes after exposure; early colonizers gram-positive cocci and rods (Actinomyces)
  • Mature biofilm: P. gingivalis, P. intermedia: the same pathogens as periodontitis
  • Pathogens may persist a year after periodontally involved teeth are extracted
  • Untreated periodontitis = contraindication; treated, arrested, compliant = OK
  • Risk assessment: before placement, during osseointegration, in maintenance, after removal
Smoking effectDetail
MicrobiologyA. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis, and B. forsythus are harder to eradicate in current smokers.
ImmunologyImpaired neutrophil chemotaxis/phagocytosis; decreased T-helper cells and B lymphocytes; increased IL-6 and TNF-α; increased collagenase activity.
PhysiologyNicotine impairs revascularization in soft and hard tissue, impairing periodontal wound healing and raising implant-failure risk.
StudyFinding
Bain & Moy 19932,194 implants: failure 11.3% smokers vs 4.76% nonsmokers
Alsaadi 2007Dose-response: worse rates in heavy smokers

Diabetes: Duration of diabetes doesn't affect implant survival under optimal glycemic control; implants are contraindicated with poorly controlled diabetes. HbA1c (last 3-4 months, the red cell's lifespan) is the gold standard.

Genetics (exam-review guide): IL-1 gene polymorphisms are linked to a hyper-responsive inflammatory reaction to microbial challenge. A positive IL-1 genotype combined with smoking has a synergistic effect — the highest risk of peri-implantitis.

sections.title: Antibiotics in perio: when, why not alone, and prescribing
sections.html:
• Bacteria (plaque) are the primary etiologic factor; antibiotics only in selected cases
  • Indications: acute infection with systemic signs (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy), aggressive periodontitis, refractory periodontitis
  • Always an adjunct to surgical and non-surgical therapy, never monotherapy; given after SRP
  • Biofilms resist antibiotics: physical barrier, β-lactamase, slowed growth (some survive 500-1000× systemic levels)
  • Bactericidal agents need dividing bacteria: never pair a bacteriostatic with a bactericidal drug
  • True allergy = hives or difficulty breathing; an upset stomach is a side effect
  • On warfarin: prescribe, but tell the physician; never change another clinician's medication
  • All: GI upset, C. diff overgrowth, weaker oral contraceptives, longer bleeding with anticoagulants; Lactobacillus and antifungals help
PrescriptionMeaning

qd / bid / tid / qidOnce / twice / three / four times a day
Must includeMedication and strength; quantity to dispense (amoxicillin 500 mg tid × 7 days = 21); Sig (instructions)

sections.html:
Local delivery agentContainsNotes
