  • Placed subgingivally at the end of SRP, after the biofilm is disrupted
  • Best indication: a localized site breaking down in an otherwise stable maintenance patient
  • Also: localized sites not responding to Phase I (generalized pockets need surgery instead)
  • Not a replacement for conventional therapy; not for aggressive periodontitis; not effective against tissue-invasive organisms
  • Can't correct the bony deformities left by disease
Host modulationNotes
RationaleBacteria are the key, the host response the engine: required but not sufficient, and the host response mediates the destruction. Not autoimmune. Deeper pockets → more bacteria → bigger response → more breakdown (a vicious cycle). Williams & Golub 1990.
The cascadePellicle within minutes of a prophy → gram-positive cocci → orange and red complexes. Complement (serum proteins): calls PMNs, histamine from mast cells (edema). Neutrophils first (24-48 h), macrophages later. Cytokines: IL-1 (osteoclast activating factor) → osteoclasts, collagenase, PGE2 → MMPs.
Step lightlyHMT down-regulates destruction and up-regulates protection, with SRP (which never removes every bacterium). Suppress the host response too far and an innocent infection can turn lethal.
NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen)Inhibit prostaglandins incl. PGE2 (upregulates osteoclastic resorption). Slowed bone loss given daily up to 3 years; daily dosing needed (a week or two does nothing). Long-term: GI problems and ulcers, hemorrhage (less platelet aggregation), renal/hepatic harm, so not developed.
BisphosphonatesInhibit osteoclasts (may be anticollagenase). BRONJ after invasive procedures (or spontaneously), mostly high-dose IV. Not an infection: scraping the dead bone is trauma, the cause, so lesions grow; in the system for years. None approved for periodontal disease.
Periostat (SDD)Sub-antimicrobial doxycycline 20 mg po bid (a fifth of the 100 mg antibiotic dose): inhibits collagenase (esp. from PMNs). First FDA-approved systemic HMT, adjunct to SRP. No antimicrobial activity, no resistance, long-term use. 1 h before/2 h after meals; avoid calcium. Contraindicated: tetracycline allergy, pregnant/lactating, children <12.
Caton 2000SRP + Periostat vs SRP + placebo: statistically significant PD and CAL gains at 3, 6, 9 months, but fractions of a mm: clinically significant? Helps refractory and aggressive cases. Efficacy beyond 9 months, safety beyond 12, not established. Consider for hard-to-modify risks (smoking, diabetes); compliance mandatory. Know the point, not the numbers.

sections.title: Recession: what predisposes, how it develops, why treat
sections.html:
Predisposing factorWhat he said
PeriodontitisAttachment and bone loss expose the root (gingivitis rarely causes recession).
TraumaToothbrushing is the most common (hard bristles or an aggressive brusher); also flossing, self-inflicted habits, foreign objects (a fingernail, a pen), caustic medicaments.
Anatomic variationsFenestration (a window in the bone), dehiscence (facial bone missing from the crest), a buccally positioned tooth. Moving that tooth back onto the arch can partly resolve recession.
Thin phenotype; lack of keratinized gingivaThin (1 mm or less, probe visible) is predisposed; under 2 mm of KG with suboptimal plaque control is at risk.
Orthodontic treatmentTeeth pushed out of the alveolar housing over thin tissue; controversial in the literature.
Previous periodontal surgeryResective surgery exposes roots on purpose, to eliminate pockets.
High muscle attachment, aberrant frenumPulls on the margin with every movement and traps plaque.
Iatrogenic restoration marginsIntrasulcular or subgingival, ill-fitting or overcontoured margins on a thin phenotype.
Smokeless tobaccoSevere localized recession where it is held, often the lower premolar or molar area.
  • Six risks of exposed roots: dentinal hypersensitivity, soft tissue discomfort, root surface caries, esthetic concerns, interference with plaque control, greater susceptibility to inflammatory insult.
  • Untreated recession continues to progress (Chambrone and Tatakis, systematic review, 2016).
  • Pathogenesis: brushing trauma (abrasion, inflammation, ulcer, recession) or plaque (the periodontitis process on a thin phenotype). The key word is inflammation; the factors only predispose.
  • Cairo RT1: about 100% coverage achievable. RT2: partial, about 50-60%, up to the interproximal attachment level. RT3: no coverage; don't graft for root coverage.

sections.title: Grafts, and which one when
sections.html:
GraftOriginNotes
Free Gingival Graft (FGG)Autograft (palate or tuberosity)Epithelium plus lamina propria in one piece. Left exposed, with an apically positioned flap: it heals into a band of keratinized gingiva. The palate heals by secondary intention.
Connective Tissue Graft (CTG, SCTG)Autograft (palate or tuberosity)Connective tissue only (trap door, or an FGG de-epithelialized). Always covered by the flap, a coronally advanced flap for root coverage; it also thickens a thin phenotype.
Acellular Dermal Matrix (ADM)Allograft (donated human dermis)Epidermis and cells removed; collagen, elastic and reticular fibers. The most common allograft. No donor site, many teeth at once; must be fully covered (no cells, no blood supply), replaced by the patient's tissue over time; doesn't work as well as autografts in demanding sites.
  • The rule: a graft covered by a flap is connective tissue only (epithelium against the flap's inner side won't heal); a graft left exposed is an FGG.
  • "We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft," tension free. A tunnel (pouch) flap reaches several teeth without raising the papillae.
  • Palate layers: epithelium 0.3-0.6 mm, lamina propria 1.25-3.0 mm, then submucosa (fat and glands, trimmed off so it doesn't slow healing). Grafts: thin 0.5-0.8 mm, average 0.9-1.4 mm, thick 1.5-2.0+ mm.
  • The greater palatine artery and nerve sit about 7 mm from the CEJ in a shallow palate, 12 mm in an average one and 17 mm in a high one: a high, deep vault gives the most room for error.
  • Sometimes an FGG is harvested but delivered as a CTG, because that is easier to harvest and heal (exam-review guide).

sections.title: Keratinized gingiva and the frenum
sections.html:
• Keratinized gingiva runs from the gingival margin to the MGJ. Find the MGJ by its color change or by rolling a probe: the mucosa rolls with it, and stops at the MGJ.
  • With plaque controlled and no traumatic factors, a zone of attached gingiva is not by itself essential (Kennedy 1985; Scheyer 2015).
  • With suboptimal plaque control, at least 2 mm of KG is needed to prevent attachment loss; under 2 mm is at risk of recession, but grafting is case by case.
  • To create KG: an FGG left exposed with an apically positioned flap. A CTG covered by alveolar mucosa gains no KG.
  • A high frenum pulls on the margin and traps plaque; a frenectomy excises it in a diamond shape, closed with sutures into the lip.
